newsitem.title: UK: Consumers may turn to govt on Brit Gas bills.
newsitem.headline: Consumers may turn to govt on Brit Gas bills.

text.p: The Gas Consumers Council said on Thursday that it would ask the government to act on mounting complaints against British Gas Plc over bills if regulator Ofgas decided it had insufficient powers.
The GCC has accused British Gas of incompetence over its new billing system, claiming that hundreds of customers in the south west of England have been mistakenly sent threatening letters this week.
The council also said the number of complaints it received about bills and unjustified reminders in the six months to September jumped 107 percent to 12,858 from a year earlier.
British Gas and Ofgas were not immediately available for comment.

The GCC said it had started talks with Ofgas after upto 1000 consumers in the south west of England ,who had switched to new suppliers, received threatening letters from British Gas's debt collection agency for bills they said they had not received.

GCC director Ian Powe said that Secretary of State for Trade and Industry Ian Lang had parallel duties with Ofgas to protect consumers. "Almost certainly in the next 10 days we'll be writing to the secretary of state if Ofgas says it can't do anything," Powe told Reuters.

Powe added repeated assurances from British Gas that it was resolving the problems "simply aren't working." He added the GCC will also ask a forthcoming parliamentary Trade & Industry select committee meeting on regulation to look at the way consumers are protected.

In a statement on Thursday, Powe accused British Gas of introducing a prototype system for billing its 18 million customers before it was fully tested. "To have done so without the normal safeguard of quality control is to risk public accusations of incompetence at a time when the company must maintain market share to survive," he said.

GCC said that on Monday and Tuesday this week, 400 customers of rival gas suppliers in the south west, which is currently the focus of an experiment on the introcduction of full competition, complained to their new suppliers about threatening letters.

"Some consumers have been so worried by the threatening tone of the letter that before talking to GCC they were on the point of phoning through their credit card numbers to the agency to pay bills they did not recognise," GCC said. It reproduced a letter from a Stockport-based debt-collection agency stressing that customers could face bailiffs, attachment of earnings orders and claims against their homes unless they paid up.
